origin: Literally per (through, by) + se (itself) — 'by itself.' Antitrust law treats certain conduct, such as price-fixing, as illegal per se, meaning courts need not examine its actual competitive effect before condemning it.

definition: Among other things; used to indicate that additional, unlisted items or matters also apply beyond those specifically mentioned.
origin: Literally inter (among) + alia (other things) — 'among other things.' A statute might state that a court may, inter alia, impose a fine, revoke a licence, or order restitution, signalling that the listed remedies are not exhaustive.

definition: The whole body of law of a particular jurisdiction or system, considered as a single organised collection.
origin: Literally corpus (body) + juris (of law) — 'body of law.' The phrase echoes the Corpus Juris Civilis, the vast compilation of Roman law codified under Emperor Justinian in the 6th century, which shaped legal systems across Europe.

origin: Literally ab (from) + initio (the beginning) — 'from the beginning.' A court that declares a contract void ab initio treats it as though it never had any legal effect at all, right from the moment it was signed.

definition: Describing a law that retroactively changes the legal consequences of actions committed before the law was enacted, especially one that criminalises past conduct.
origin: Literally ex (from, out of) + post (after) + facto (the fact, deed) — 'from after the fact.' Many constitutions ban ex post facto criminal laws, preventing the government from punishing someone for conduct that was legal when they did it.

definition: Acting in the place of a parent, taking on a parent's responsibilities and authority for the care, welfare, and discipline of a child or student.
origin: Literally in (in) + loco (the place) + parentis (of a parent) — 'in the place of a parent.' Schools and boarding institutions often act in loco parentis while a child is in their care, assuming a duty to supervise and protect the student's welfare.

definition: With the necessary changes having been made; used to indicate that a rule, comparison, or precedent applies equally to a different situation once minor adjustments are made for the differences.
origin: Literally mutatis (having been changed) + mutandis (things needing to be changed) — 'with things changed that need to be changed.' A clause might state that the same procedure applies to a related dispute, mutatis mutandis, meaning with whatever small adjustments the different facts require.

definition: Made or done in good faith; genuine, sincere, and without intent to deceive.
origin: Literally bona (good) + fide (faith) — 'in good faith.' A bona fide purchaser buys property honestly, for value, without knowledge of any defect in the seller's title, and is often protected by law even if the seller's title later proves flawed.
